Volume 17 · Chapter 04

Designing a graduate seminar

Professional Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v17-c03

By the endOrganize a research seminar around questions, methods and scholarly disagreement.

A graduate seminar should leave participants able to reconstruct an argument, locate a consequential disagreement and design a feasible next investigation. A procession of slide summaries does not establish those capabilities.

Capability and prerequisites. Organize a research seminar around questions, methods and scholarly disagreement. Build on course design, literature mapping, reproduction and referee reasoning. Participants in this specimen need conditional expectations, potential outcomes, finite probability mixtures and elementary identification arguments from Volume 12. The course supplies a diagnostic and repair route; graduate enrollment is not evidence of those prerequisites. Every syllabus, case, dialogue and proposed assessment below is original instructional material. No seminar attendance, learning gain or real research result is claimed.

1. Select an argument sequence, not a reputation list

A research question specifies an unresolved object of inquiry. An estimand is the mathematical target; an identification argument explains why a stated observation law and assumptions determine it, or constrain it to a set. A presentation reconstructs the claim and its support for an audience. A discussion tests consequences and alternatives. A critique identifies a specific claim, a consequential problem and a warranted repair. A proposal commits to a tractable question, method, evidence and failure conditions. These are different performances; one polished talk cannot replace all of them.

Select a small connected set of papers by solving their central problem yourself. Record question, target, data or theoretical primitives, assumptions, argumentative step, unresolved issue and the next paper's role. Prefer a paper whose key result can be reconstructed within the available time to an impressive title whose machinery the group cannot yet use. Check access and version before assigning it. A working manuscript may differ from the final article; record the actual version. Teach missing prerequisites or narrow the required section. Do not label an unread paper a completed review.

A useful disagreement may concern a theorem's validity, an assumption's credibility, the target population, or the decision that the target informs. Locate the level before staging a debate. Two correct statements about different estimands are not a mathematical contradiction. Conversely, “both perspectives are valuable” is inadequate when one derivation is wrong. Ask each side to state the strongest defensible opposing argument, then identify what evidence or assumption would change its position.

The Bok Center's syllabus guidance informs the explicit course arrangements below; Carnegie Mellon's alignment guidance informs matching reading, practice and assessment. These are reused bounded professional recommendations, not experimental evidence that our seminar design works. The role rotation and workload are proposed local choices.

2. Complete specimen syllabus: Which policy effect do we learn?

Purpose, audience and duration. Six weekly two-hour meetings for a small graduate methods seminar, with six planned independent hours each week. The topic is the relationship between treatment-effect identification and a policy target. Objectives: S1 reconstruct a finite identification or sharpness proof; S2 distinguish observed comparisons, local receipt effects and population interventions; S3 deliver a supported critique and a faithful response; S4 produce a verifiable proof-reconstruction dossier; S5 defend a feasible, bounded research proposal. The course is an intensive module, not a complete field survey or proof of original research achievement.

Entry diagnostic and answer. Before week 1 ask: “A population contains equal masses with outcomes 2 and 6. What is its mean? Does observing outcome 6 after treatment reveal that person's untreated outcome? What extra argument makes a bound sharp?” Answers: mean 4; no, the untreated potential outcome remains missing; every value in the claimed identified set must be achievable under the observations and restrictions, not merely satisfy an inequality. A participant who cannot form the mixture revisits expectation and the worked mixtures below. A missing-counterfactual or sharpness error routes to econometric foundations and a guided two-world construction before independent proof work. This is targeted preparation, not exclusion based on one aggregate score.

Required research readings and selection record. R1 is Guido Imbens and Joshua Angrist, Identification and Estimation of Local Average Treatment Effects, Econometrica 62(2), 1994, printed pages 467–475. Its central role is the identification of an effect for people whose receipt changes with an instrument; required close reading is Sections 1–2, including Conditions 1–2 and Theorem 1. Section 3's general instrument weights and asymptotic analysis are extension reading, not an unannounced examination requirement. Section 4 supplies assumption-analysis practice, not evidence that an instrument in our fictional case is valid.

R2 is Alexander Balke and Judea Pearl, Bounds on Treatment Effects from Studies with Imperfect Compliance, the UCLA repository manuscript marked “To appear in JASA,” with ten printed manuscript pages plus a repository cover. Required close reading is Sections 1–2, printed pages 1–3, and Section 5, printed page 9; inspect the beginning of Section 3 to locate the finite response-type strategy. The repository's 2011 deposit date is not treated as the article's publication year. The chapter does not assert this manuscript is identical to the final published article.

R2 argues for population-effect bounds when local responses need not answer an eventual policy question. Its conclusion criticizes an instrument-dependent target, while R1 establishes a local identification result. The seminar must distinguish that policy objection from refuting R1's theorem. R2's discussion specifically names the later Angrist–Imbens–Rubin formulation; the chosen R1 is the earlier identification foundation, not falsely described as a direct reply. We do not adopt the blanket proposition that a local effect is useless for every policy. The cases below ask when the intervention resembles the experiment. The full general binary-instrument bound formulas and the papers' empirical applications are outside the required reconstruction. No published data, table or numerical result is copied into these original exercises.

Six-week syllabus, with a concrete product and feedback owner
Week and questionRequired preparationMeeting and productFeedback and dependency

2. When is a bound the complete answer?Case 1 proof and R2 Section 5; locate Section 3's response-type strategy without assuming its formulas proved hereCase 1 discussion; paired reconstruction then individual changed-data proof.Discussant returns one consequential objection; instructor checks sharpness, not only endpoints.

Which effect does an instrument identify?R1 Sections 1–2; write each assumption before the ratioCase 2 presentation and compliance decomposition; submit reconstruction draft with version and discrepancy log.Instructor checks the ratio and target before policy proposal; reviewer attempts an alternative world.

Workload and capacity. Weekly (meeting, close reading, reconstruction, writing/preparation) hours are (2,2,2,2), giving (8,48) hours weekly and across six weeks. In week 5 the six independent hours become one reading, two reconstruction and three proposal revision; in week 6 one reading, one independent proof check and four defense/proposal preparation. These replace other homework. Paper length is not a reliable time estimate; check the first two weeks' actual workload and narrow optional sections before adding tasks. With six participants, six twelve-minute defenses use 72 of 120 minutes, leaving 48 for framing, breaks and synthesis. A larger cohort requires additional meeting capacity or smaller groups with equal individual evidence; do not silently shorten every challenge.

Roles and operating arrangements. For each paper meeting designate a presenter, discussant, reconstruction lead and chair/recorder; rotate named assignments before launch so everyone presents and critiques once and submits an individual proof and proposal. For six participants, two present in weeks 2, 3 and 4, each with a twelve-minute talk within the 120-minute meeting; use written discussant notes to give every participant a critique opportunity. The 60-minute Case 1 workshop below is one block within that meeting, leaving another hour for the additional talk, discussion and synthesis. Publish the roster, actual dates, instructor contact, weekly support hour, submission route, access arrangements and locally applicable policies before enrollment; those real logistics are not invented here. Required external papers must be lawfully accessible to all participants. If access fails, supply a lawful institutional route or change the reading and its assessment; the offline chapter's cases do not pretend to be the source paper.

Submit a question note before the meeting: one claim, its precise source location, one reconstructed step and one consequential question. A presenter submits an argument map, not slides alone. A discussant sends a short written critique early enough for the presenter to understand it, but keeps the independently assessed changed-assumption task unseen. The chair protects time for reasoning, asks participants to distinguish disagreement from misunderstanding and records unresolved issues. Allow quiet written preparation and equivalent written reasoning where spontaneous speech is not the construct; the scheduled defense still assesses explaining and responding, with actual access arrangements agreed in advance. Assess contributions for their reasoning, not speaking frequency, accent or willingness to dominate.

Assessment. Proposed course-mark weights are reading/question notes 15%, presentation plus response 20%, discussant critique 15%, reconstruction dossier 25%, and proposal plus individual defense 25%, recorded as (15,20,15,25,25); total 100%. Each uses accuracy, explicit assumptions, inspectable support and response to a substantive challenge. The reconstruction must contain a correct proof and a reproducible independent check; the proposal must specify a target, credible evidence or theorem strategy and a feasible route. An unresolved critical identification or provenance error blocks an “independently ready” judgment regardless of mark. These local rules are proposals to align with actual course policy, not institutional requirements or a psychometric scale.

Reading notes and presentations may use cited resources and declared tools; preserve draft arguments, calculations and revisions. Independent transfer proofs and defenses require the learner's own reasoning without outside generated answers. Document assistance rather than mislabeling it independent. Arrange missed work and equivalent reassessment under published local rules; give a response deadline and instructor owner for each feedback cycle. Return one major reasoning issue with a concrete next task, retain both attempts, and check the revised skill on a new case. The final project is a feasible proposal and reconstruction, not a promised publishable discovery.

3. Worked seminar: a population effect without a selection assumption

Case 1 — Reconstruct, challenge and revise a bound

Task and units. A fictional training program may change an enterprise's weekly production score. Potential scores Y(1) and Y(0) lie in the known interval [0,10]; this is a substantive outcome-scale restriction, not the smallest/largest score happened to be sampled. D indicates actual participation, Y=DY(1)+(1−D)Y(0), and there are no spillovers. Treat the supplied distribution as the exact population law, with no sampling uncertainty. The primitive (participation share p, observed participant mean m₁, observed nonparticipant mean m₀, lower support, upper support) is (2/5,7,4,0,10). Target τ=E[Y(1)−Y(0)] is the effect of supplying training to everyone rather than no one in this population, in score units per enterprise. No random selection or mean independence is assumed. Derive the entire compatible range, prove attainability, then evaluate the claim “the observed three-unit difference establishes a positive effect.”

Derivation. Let u=E[Y(1)|D=0] and v=E[Y(0)|D=1] be the missing means. By partitioning the population, E[Y(1)]=pm₁+(1−p)u and E[Y(0)]=(1−p)m₀+pv. Therefore τ=pm₁−(1−p)m₀+(1−p)u−pv. The observed component is 2/5, so τ=2/5+(3/5)u−(2/5)v. Because u,v∈[0,10], minimize with u=0,v=10 and maximize with u=10,v=0. The full result (observed difference, lower effect, upper effect, width) is (3,-18/5,32/5,10). A positive observed difference is compatible with a negative effect.

Sharpness proof, including interiors. Keep the observed conditional outcome distributions fixed. For every nonparticipant set the missing treated score to u; for every participant set the missing untreated score to v. These assignments obey consistency and support and do not alter any observation. The lower and upper assignments attain the endpoints. For any λ∈[0,1], choose u=10λ and v=10(1−λ), yielding τ=−18/5+10λ; thus every intermediate value is attainable. If scores were restricted to integer individuals in a fixed small population, the attainable set could be discrete; our population-law model permits these real scores or mixtures. We prove sharpness for exactly this model, not for unknown additional restrictions.

Changed assumption. Mean independence of each potential score from D would set u=m₁=7 and v=m₀=4, yielding τ=3. This is an additional identification restriction, not an arithmetic correction. Under the different restriction Y(1)≥Y(0) for every enterprise, τ≥0; zero is attained by setting each missing outcome equal to its observed counterpart, while the former upper construction still obeys monotone response. Mixtures preserve that restriction, so the sharp range is (0,32/5). Monotone response of outcomes is distinct from monotone receipt under an encouragement in Case 2.

Complete 60-minute teaching artifact. Minutes 0–8: individual missing-mean definition and units check. 8–20: presenter derives the partition identity while participants mark which terms are observed. 20–32: pairs construct the two endpoint worlds, followed by each person's interior argument. 32–45: discussant challenges the selection assumption using the memo below. 45–55: participants independently derive the monotone-response variant. 55–60: exit sentence naming what changes and what remains unverified. The instructor's expected answers are the calculations and constructions above; a wider interval without a sharpness argument is incomplete.

Full specimen discussant memo. “The presenter correctly calculates the observed mean difference 7−4=3, but uses it as the effect of universal training. One sufficient justification would set the missing means equal to the corresponding observed means; the supplied data do not warrant that restriction or another argument eliminating selection bias. In the permitted model, setting u=0,v=10 preserves every observation and gives τ=−18/5. This is a consequential counterexample to the sign claim, not evidence that training actually harms production. Replace the causal point claim with [−18/5,32/5], supply the endpoint and interior constructions, and state a sufficient selection restriction under which 3 is identified. If the proposal instead asserts monotone response, explain why it is credible and report the resulting [0,32/5] without treating the assertion as verified.”

Full specimen presenter response. “I accept the target error. My difference of observed means does not fill the two missing means. I have replaced the point claim, added the two full populations and the λ construction, and kept the 3-unit result only under explicitly stated mean independence. I can derive monotone-response bounds, but the supplied observations do not establish that restriction. My next proposal will identify which information could constrain the missing terms rather than merely collect more copies of the same selected comparison.” This is a model response, not an observed student's revision.

Rubric and follow-up. On a proposed ten-point task, give target/units 2, partition algebra 2, endpoints 2, sharpness including interiors 2, and defensible critique/response 2. Give targeted feedback to an answer with correct endpoints but no construction: “Show a population that leaves m₁,m₀,p unchanged and attains an arbitrary intermediate value.” On the later changed dataset in Exercise 3, require an individual proof. Fluent discussion or copying the displayed λ cannot establish independent reconstruction.

4. Worked seminar: local identification and a different policy

Case 2 — A complete presentation, critique and proposal revision

Contract. Z∈{0,1} is randomized encouragement with both values having positive probability, independent of the joint potential receipt and outcome variables. D(z) is receipt if encouragement is z. Assume consistency, no interference, and exclusion: Z affects Y only through D. Outcomes are weekly production scores in [0,10]. Receipt is monotone D(1)≥D(0); the probability of compliers is positive. “Always” means D(0)=D(1)=1, “complier” means (0,1), and “never” means (0,0). Defiers (1,0) are excluded by this assumption, not by observing a positive average first stage.

Original instructor population; the two unobserved noncomplier outcomes are not identified by encouragement data
TypeMassD(0)D(1)Y(0)Y(1)
Always1/41146
Complier1/20125
Never1/40010

The complete rows (mass,D(0),D(1),Y(0),Y(1)) are ((1/4,1,1,4,6),(1/2,0,1,2,5),(1/4,0,0,1,0)). These are synthetic potential-outcome inputs for an instructor check. Real encouragement data do not reveal each person's type and both outcomes. The seminar task is to derive the observable distributions, identify the local effect, and then remove access to the unobserved always-type Y(0) and never-type Y(1) before making a population claim.

Complete proof and answer. Independence and consistency imply E[D|Z=1]−E[D|Z=0]=E[D(1)−D(0)]=pC. Exclusion gives E[Y|Z=1]−E[Y|Z=0]=E[(D(1)−D(0))(Y(1)−Y(0))]=pCE[Y(1)−Y(0)|C]. Always and never types contribute zero to the difference; monotonicity removes a negative-weight defier term. Division by positive pC identifies the complier effect, not the average over everyone. This binary proof reconstructs the central logic of R1's Theorem 1 under our explicitly stated contract; it does not prove its more general weighting or inference results.

For the table, (receipt at Z=0, receipt at Z=1, mean outcome at Z=0, mean outcome at Z=1) is (1/4,3/4,11/4,17/4). Thus (first stage, reduced form, local effect, instructor population ATE) is (1/2,3/2,3,7/4). The final 7/4 uses both unobserved noncomplier outcomes from the instructor table. It is not identified merely because the writer can see those synthetic inputs.

Observation-equivalent worlds and a sharp population range. Let a denote the always-type untreated mean and n the never-type treated mean. Observed always-type treated mean is 6, observed never-type untreated mean is 1, and complier means are 2 and 5; these stratum means can be recovered from the conditional joint receipt/outcome law under the assumptions, by removing the always and never mixtures. For example, Z=0,D=1 contains only always types; Z=1,D=0 only never types. Receipt rates recover masses 1/4,1/2,1/4. Removing their contributions from aggregate outcomes recovers the two complier means.

Population τ=(1/4)(6−a)+(1/2)(5−2)+(1/4)(n−1)=11/4+(n−a)/4. With a,n∈[0,10], the sharp ATE range is (1/4,21/4). Lower endpoint a=10,n=0 and upper endpoint a=0,n=10 leave each observed outcome under both encouragement values unchanged; any interior follows by mixing these unobserved values while leaving the observed distributions fixed. The supplied instructor world a=4,n=0 gives 7/4 inside the range. The same local effect 3 therefore coexists with materially different population effects. This simple stratum proof is our original bounded-outcome special case, not a transcription or verification of R2's general binary-response formulas.

Policy comparison with full accounting. Suppose each actual receipt costs 2 score-equivalent resource units, and encouragement 1 costs an additional 1/5 per enterprise compared with encouragement 0. The input (receipt cost, extra encouragement cost) is (2,1/5). These are stated welfare conversion assumptions, not observed prices. Keeping the same population, encouragement mechanism, exclusion and outcomes, moving Z from 0 to 1 has expected net change ΔY−2ΔD−1/5=3/10. A hypothetical intervention that supplies treatment to everyone versus no one instead has net τ−2, bounded by (-7/4,13/4). In the instructor world it equals −1/4. A local positive net effect per induced receipt does not settle the universal policy. Nor does this model establish that either intervention is lawful, acceptable or feasible; actual receipt constraints and stakeholder consent belong in a proposal's feasibility assessment.

Exclusion stress test. Add a direct outcome increment κ=1/2 to every enterprise assigned Z=1, retaining the table's receipt effects and receipt behavior. Now ΔY=2 and the ratio becomes 4, although the receipt effect for compliers remains 3; (1/2,2,4,3) records κ, changed reduced form, ratio and receipt effect. All realized scores in this construction stay within [0,10]. Randomization still identifies the total encouragement contrast, but exclusion no longer justifies interpreting the ratio as the receipt effect. This is an alternative data-generating world, not a claim that the original full observed law remains fixed.

Complete presentation outline, twelve minutes. Minutes 0–2: define the proposed policy and distinguish Z from D. 2–5: write the assumptions and prove the two differences using compliance types. 5–8: calculate the observed moments and local effect from the table. 8–10: hide a,n and construct the two ATE endpoints. 10–12: compare the encouragement and universal-policy net results and name the remaining feasibility question. A faithful talk concludes: “The same encouragement identifies its own outcome contrast; additional assumptions identify a local receipt effect. Neither gives the missing noncomplier effects for universal receipt.”

Full discussant challenge and reply. Discussant: “Your headline says training should be supplied to everyone because 3 exceeds cost 2. But 3 averages only over induced recipients. In the compatible a=10,n=0 world, the population effect is 1/4 and universal net value is −7/4. Change the headline or defend a restriction on a,n. Also explain what happens if the encouragement itself changes output.” Presenter: “I withdraw the universal recommendation. I retain the 3/10 net comparison for this same encouragement under its stated cost and invariance assumptions. I report universal net bounds instead. The direct-effect construction makes the ratio 4 without changing complier receipt effects, so a new study needs evidence about that pathway; random assignment alone cannot close it.” This evaluates the consequence of the objection rather than its rhetorical force.

Full proposal artifact. “Question: can an economically defensible restriction on noncomplier outcomes resolve the sign of universal net value in this bounded production model? Target: E[Y(1)−Y(0)]−2 for the stated population, separate from the encouragement target. Method: first reconstruct the compliance decomposition and sharp unrestricted interval, then add a transparent proposed bound a−n≤2. Because τ=11/4−(a−n)/4, this restriction implies τ≥9/4 and universal net≥1/4. Construct compatible endpoint worlds and test logical compatibility with observed outcomes; do not treat compatibility as evidence that the restriction holds. Evidence plan: identify what safe, consensual design or external evidence could inform the currently missing means, document lawful access and population comparability, and obtain qualified review before any data collection. If those requirements cannot be met within six weeks, deliver the theoretical sensitivity map and an explicit unavailable-evidence statement instead of a fake empirical estimate. Timeline: week4 target/access memo, week5 independently checked proof and objection, week6 revised proposal/defense. Contribution: a bounded seminar investigation; novelty relative to the selected literature remains to be established through additional reading. Failure trigger: inability to justify a−n≤2 means the original sign ambiguity remains.”

The proposed restriction is consequential: its threshold for strictly positive universal net is a−n<3. Equality gives zero, and a−n>3 gives a negative value. The proposal's new interval under a−n≤2 is (1/4,13/4); a=2,n=0 and a=0,n=10 attain its endpoints. The restriction itself remains hypothetical. A proper next study would defend it or replace it with a feasible measurement strategy, not merely choose it to obtain a preferred conclusion.

Evaluation. Proposed ten points: target/assumptions 2; compliance proof 2; observed moments and ratio 2; counterexample plus cost accounting 2; supported response and feasible proposal 2. A correct ratio cannot compensate for a universal recommendation unsupported by the missing effects. Require an individual changed compliance distribution after the prepared talk.

5. Make reconstruction and critique inspectable

A proof reconstruction restates a result in a declared notation, supplies every logical step and checks its assumptions. A numerical verification on synthetic data can detect arithmetic errors but cannot prove a general identity. A computational reproduction reruns a specified analysis on its supplied data/environment; a new synthetic table is not reproduction of a paper's empirical result. This module requires the former, with an independent finite check. Actual empirical replication is an optional later project requiring lawful data, documented transformations and an appropriate comparison. Do not promise a restricted-data replication by week 5 without access.

Complete reconstruction assignment. Reconstruct R1's binary Theorem 1 logic using the Case 2 contract; submit (i) source/version and precise theorem/page reference; (ii) notation mapping and all observation/behavior assumptions; (iii) the complete cancellation/division proof; (iv) a hand calculation plus an independently implemented enumeration of the supplied synthetic types; (v) one failed-assumption witness; and (vi) a discrepancy log, result status and individual response to review. State interpreter/version and actual execution status if code is used. The expected outputs are the observed/effect vectors above; a run producing ATE=3 has confused targets. An appropriate log would say “Expected LATE3 and full-table ATE7/4 differ because the targets weight different types; this is not a replication failure.” A hypothetical log is a template until someone actually runs the submitted program.

What counts as completion? A reviewer should reconstruct the proof without the presenter's narration, independently recover the finite moments, and inspect the counterexample and source mapping. Preserve submitted code, inputs and output with versions and discrepancies if execution occurs. “Runnable” means it can be attempted, “executed” requires an actual recorded run, and “matched” requires comparison to the declared target. The present library's author validation does not count as a learner's submission. If the learner uses only exact hand calculation, describe it as such and arrange the separately required independent finite check; do not invent a software log.

Feedback procedure. Quote or locate the contested claim, say why it matters, provide a counterexample or missing step, and request the smallest substantive correction. Distinguish a fatal target error from a typo. The recipient must either make the correction and trace its consequences or defend the original with evidence. The chair records unresolved disagreements as separate claims with proposed tests; voting or prestige does not settle a theorem. Invite a written follow-up when an answer needs time, while preserving an unseen independent challenge for assessment.

Exercises

  1. Write a complete two-paper selection memo using R1 and R2: question, exact required sections, each paper's function, the disagreement and one scope/access limit. Explain why “one famous paper each week” would not establish a seminar sequence.
  2. Prepare a complete 30-minute discussion plan for Case 1, including actual opening question, a missing-mean task, a consequential challenge, expected answers and an exit criterion. Preserve individual reasoning rather than using all time for presenter summary.
  3. Change Case 1's primitive tuple to (3/5,8,3,0,10). Derive the sharp range, supply endpoint and interior worlds, compare the observed difference, and recompute under monotone outcome response.
  4. A reconstruction labels the Case 2 ratio “population effect” and reports 3 as both LATE and ATE. Write a complete discrepancy entry and corrective feedback. Recompute the true instructor-table ATE and give one observation-equivalent world that changes it while keeping the ratio fixed.
  5. A presenter argues that a positive first stage proves monotone receipt. Consider type masses (complier,defier,always,never)=(2/5,1/10,1/5,3/10), with type-specific receipt effects (2,8,0,0). Let complier and defier untreated outcomes be0, always outcomes(1,1), never outcomes(1,1). Z is independent and excluded. Calculate first stage, reduced form and ratio. Explain precisely why the local interpretation fails.
  6. For a separate mean-only sensitivity exercise, observed reduced form is3/4 and first stage1/4; the maintained structural equation is ΔY=pCτC+κ with no defiers, and the unverified direct-effect restriction is κ∈[0,1/4]. The ordered input (reduced form, first stage, direct lower, direct upper) is (3/4,1/4,0,1/4). Derive the compatible τC interval and give the corrected two-sentence interpretation. Explain why it is not a confidence interval or proof of exclusion.
  7. A proposed week assigns 2 meeting hours, 3 close-reading, 2 reconstruction and 3 proposal writing against the syllabus's eight-hour ceiling. Give an exact feasible reallocation and a full notice identifying a substantive scope change, the protected learning evidence and what will be checked after implementation.
  8. Write a complete response letter and revised proposal decision for the Case 2 proposal after a reviewer says: “You have no evidence for a−n≤2 and your new external dataset has no documented access permission.” Include the mathematical consequence, a feasible six-week deliverable, what actual evidence would be needed next and what the current seminar cannot certify.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

1. Selection memo

“Our question is whether an identified response to encouragement answers a universal-treatment policy question. Read R1 Sections1–2/printed467–470 to reconstruct instrument assumptions and the local-effect proof; use Section4 for assumption challenges. Read R2 manuscript Sections1–2/printed1–3 and Section5/printed9 to compare its population target and policy criticism. R1 establishes an effect for induced recipients; R2 motivates bounding a population effect when that target is insufficient. A valid local theorem and an unresolved population decision can coexist. We will derive our own finite cases, not claim to reproduce R2's general formulas or either paper's empirical applications. Confirm lawful access and the exact repository manuscript before assigning it; deposit date does not establish publication date.” Evaluate concrete question, page/section scope, method-target connection, faithful disagreement and access/version limit. Fame supplies none of these links.

2. Actual discussion plan

Minutes0–4: each participant answers “Which two conditional means are unobserved?” Expected u=E[Y1|D0],v=E[Y0|D1]. 4–12: pairs write τ=2/5+3u/5−2v/5; each person explains one weight. 12–20: ask “Can the same observed data have a negative effect?” Expected u0,v10 gives−18/5 while u10,v0 gives32/5; the chair asks how observations remain fixed. 20–26: discussant asks whether every interior value is attainable; expected u10λ,v10(1−λ) yields−18/5+10λ. 26–30: independent exit asks what extra restriction yields3 and whether this exercise verifies it. Answer: mean independence fixes u7,v4; no, it was stipulated. Full credit requires a complete30minute allocation, precise questions/answers, an individual response and a criterion checking reasoning; an attendance tally is inadequate.

3. Changed sharp bound

Now the observed component is(3/5)8−(2/5)3=18/5, so τ=18/5+(2/5)u−(3/5)v. The sharp interval is[−12/5,38/5], while the observed difference is5. Lower worldu0,v10 and upper worldu10,v0 preserve the observed groups; u10λ,v10(1−λ) yields−12/5+10λ. Monotone outcome response gives[0,38/5]: the zero world fills each missing outcome with its observed counterpart, the upper world respects monotonicity, and mixtures attain all intervening means. The result vector (observed difference, unrestricted lower/upper, monotone lower/upper) is (5,-12/5,38/5,0,38/5). Score target/algebra, both constructions, interior sharpness and the distinction between observed difference and assumed identification. Merely truncating a bound at zero without constructing feasible worlds is incomplete.

4. Discrepancy and correction

Entry: “Target mismatch in output labels: ratio3 estimates the complier effect under the stated contract. Full instructor-table ATE is(1/4)2+(1/2)3+(1/4)(−1)=7/4. These are different targets, so equality is not an expected check.” Feedback: “Replace the ATE label on the ratio, calculate the full-table average separately, then explain which entries encouragement data cannot reveal.” One alternate world changes always Y0 to0 and never Y1 to10, leaving every observed outcome unchanged and yieldingATE21/4, stillLATE3. The checked pair is (7/4,21/4). A complete response records the corrected interpretation and downstream policy claim, not merely a changed printed number; a log must not say code was run unless it was.

5. Positive relevance with defiers

The first stage is2/5−1/10=3/10. The reduced form is(2/5)2−(1/10)8=0. Hence the ratio is0, giving (3/10,0,0). Both compliers and defiers have positive receipt effects, but defier contribution enters with the opposite sign because encouragement reduces their receipt. Always/never contributions cancel. A positive average first stage means more positive than negative receipt changes in mass, not no negative changes. The no-defier hypothesis is false in these primitives, so the ratio does not identify the complier effect2. Expected outcomes under Z0 andZ1 are both13/10; receipt rates are3/10 and3/5. All scores obey[0,10]. Full credit requires the cancellation, the exact distinction between average and individual monotonicity and an explicit corrective statement.

6. Direct-path sensitivity

τC=(3/4−κ)/(1/4)=3−4κ, so the interval is (2,3). “Under the stated mean equation and direct-path restriction, local receipt effects from2to3 are compatible with the supplied contrasts. The bound onκ is an assumption not established by these two numbers, and no sampling confidence level has been supplied.” Each endpoint and interior can be obtained by its correspondingκ in this mean-only model; additional observed distributions or outcome restrictions would need separate compatibility checks. Settingκ=0 recovers3 but does not prove exclusion. Evaluate algebra, decreasing endpoint order, scope and uncertainty interpretation.

7. Workload notice

Original demand10 exceeds8 by2. A revised allocation is(meeting,reading,reconstruction,writing)=(2,2,2,2), recorded with total/excess as (10,2,2,2,2,2). Notice: “This week's required reading is now the stated identification sections and one page locating the policy target; general multivalued weighting and asymptotic proofs remain optional and unassessed. Submit a one-page proposal checkpoint rather than a polished full draft; move that polishing into week6's already budgeted preparation. We retain the independent binary proof and failed-assumption witness. At the next meeting we will review actual time and errors, and further narrow unassessed breadth if the eight-hour estimate is unrealistic.” Full credit requires an exact nonnegative budget, named scope changes, protected evidence and a check of actual feasibility. Reprinting eight hours beside unchanged tasks is not a repair.

8. Full response and proposal decision

“Thank you for separating mathematical compatibility from evidence. I withdraw the empirical defense of a−n≤2 and the implied guaranteed positive universal net. With only the stated support and observed law, universal net remains[−7/4,13/4]; choosing a−n<3 would ensure a positive sign algebraically, but its credibility is exactly the missing issue. I will not access or redistribute an undocumented external dataset. By week6 I will submit a proof-reconstruction dossier, the sharp unrestricted interval, a sensitivity map in a−n, and a revised study protocol listing required variables, population link, access permissions and identification threats. A future empirical phase requires lawful access, relevant measurements or intervention design, qualified review and evidence supporting any restriction; those requirements are currently pending. This seminar can assess my bounded reasoning and feasibility planning, not certify a new empirical finding, originality or completed human-subject approval.” Decision: accept the narrower theoretical proposal for further assessment if its proof and independent defense pass; defer the empirical phase. Full credit requires a concrete withdrawal, correct mathematical consequence, useful feasible deliverable and precise evidence/status boundaries.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to an instructor why R1 and R2 can generate a productive seminar without declaring one author wrong. Answer guide: identify local versus population target, reconstruct the assumptions for each, use Case2's same observations/differentATE worlds, and ask which intervention the decision actually concerns. A discussion that never checks the proof or target is only a preference exchange. Judge the accurate reconstruction and consequential question, not rhetorical confidence.

Delayed task. Without these solutions, a new population has masses(always,complier,never)=(1/5,3/5,1/5), with potential-score pairs(3,4),(1,3),(2,2). Its rows (mass,D0,D1,Y0,Y1) are ((1/5,1,1,3,4),(3/5,0,1,1,3),(1/5,0,0,2,2)). Derive receipt and outcome contrasts, local effect and full-tableATE, then say whether the last is observed from encouragement alone. Full answer: receipt means1/5,4/5; outcome means9/5,3; first stage3/5; reduced form6/5; local effect2; full-tableATE7/5. The result vector is (1/5,4/5,9/5,3,3/5,6/5,2,7/5). The ATE calculation uses missing noncomplier outcomes; without those instructor inputs it is not identified. Require a fresh independently explained counterexample if the learner has memorized this answer.

Sources, scope and next work

R1 was freshly read on all nine rendered pages, including proofs and the limits of estimated-instrument inference; only the declared binary identification portion is required here. R2's repository body was read for its problem formulation, assumptions and policy conclusion; corrupted mathematical text extraction and failed image retrieval prevent claiming a complete equation or empirical audit. The chapter therefore teaches and proves its own transparent finite special cases, and does not reproduce the paper's general bounds or empirical results. Teaching-center records retain their original coordinator inspection attribution. External papers are linked, not redistributed in this offline edition.

A real seminar needs actual participant work, feedback and a qualified observer before anyone can claim teaching effectiveness or independent research competence. The next chapters develop assessment and feedback; a later field seminar can add lawful empirical replication, sampling uncertainty, general response-type optimization and current research after the relevant prerequisites and source inspections. This six-week module establishes a bounded argument-and-proposal practice, not exhaustive command of the treatment-effects literature.

Sources and further study

  • Harvard Derek Bok Center — Syllabus Design — Professional benchmark for complete and clear course communication.
  • Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center — Align Assessments, Objectives, Instructional Strategies — Narrow guidance that evidence tasks and practice should match intended capability; original economic examples separately constructed.
  • Guido W. Imbens, Joshua D. Angrist — Identification and Estimation of Local Average Treatment Effects (Econometrica62(2), March1994, pages467–475) — Binary heterogeneous treatment effects, compliance decomposition and LATE limits. Original finite population and violations are not attributed to the paper.
  • Alexander Balke and Judea Pearl — Bounds on Treatment Effects from Studies with Imperfect Compliance (UCLA repository manuscript marked To appear in JASA) — Actual research reading: population-effect target, maintained exclusion/random assignment setup, and stated policy objection to an instrument-dependent local target. Seminar asks whether that objection applies to the particular intervention; it does not declare the LATE theorem refuted.
